text: Reading about circuits is not the same skill as predicting what one will do before you run it. This lab closes out the chapter by having you build a 3-qubit entangled state, commit to a prediction in advance, and check it against a real run.

The GHZ state generalizes the Bell state to three qubits: superposition on qubit 0, then a chain of CX gates entangling the rest onto it. Before running anything, pause and predict which of the 8 possible 3-bit outcomes you expect, and roughly in what proportion.

h(0) splits qubit 0 into superposition. cx(0,1) says if qubit 0 is 1, flip qubit 1 — so qubit 1 now always matches qubit 0. cx(1,2) says if qubit 1 is 1, flip qubit 2 — so qubit 2 now always matches qubit 1, and therefore qubit 0 as well. That reasoning should lead you to predict exactly two outcomes, 000 and 111, each roughly half the time, with the other six combinations never appearing.

The math confirms it directly: the circuit produces exactly the sum of |000> and |111>, divided by the square root of 2 — amplitude 0.7071068 on each, and exactly zero on all six other combinations. That gives ideal probabilities P(000)=0.5, P(111)=0.5, and zero everywhere else.

A real seeded run at 2048 shots gives something like 000: 1069, 111: 979, with all six other outcomes at exactly zero. The 1069-versus-979 split is ordinary shot noise. But the six missing outcomes staying at exactly zero, with no exceptions, is the structural signature of genuine entanglement — if a real run ever showed a nonzero count there, that would be a sign of a bug or genuine hardware noise, not something to shrug off.
Chapter 3 looks closely at the backend you've been running against all along: the Qiskit Aer simulator itself, and the real choices it offers once circuits get more demanding.
